question: Plasmodium vivax, a common malaria parasite, thrives across tropical Asia but is nearly absent from West Africa. Why?
answer: A blood type. Most West and Central Africans are Duffy-negative: their red cells lack the surface protein vivax grips to get in. Miller and colleagues showed it in 1976 with volunteers. The shield leaks: vivax has since been found infecting Duffy-negative people in Madagascar.
move: Before crediting the famous cause, check the cases it cannot explain.
ask: Which explanation do I trust because it is famous, not because it fits every case?

clues.text: Vivax is common in South and Southeast Asia, just as hot and wet.
Falciparum, a deadlier malaria carried by the same mosquitoes, is rife there.
Most West Africans lack the sickle-cell gene. They escape vivax all the same.
Vivax enters red cells by gripping the Duffy protein. Most there lack it.

scene.why: The famous shield, sickle cell, is missing in most of them. A missing Duffy protein is not.

reference: Miller, Mason, Clyde & McGinniss, The resistance factor to Plasmodium vivax in blacks: the Duffy-blood-group genotype, FyFy, New England Journal of Medicine, 1976
